# What happens when you edit a generated file

Ferrum owns some files outright — the nginx vhosts it renders, the PHP-FPM pool
files, the logrotate fragments. They live under directories of the panel's own
(`/etc/nginx/ferrum.d/`), and each one starts with a line naming the SHA-256 of
the rest of the file:

```nginx
# FERRUM-MANAGED sha256:9f2c…
# generated by Ferrum — edits are detected, not overwritten
server {
    …
```

## If you edit one

Nothing breaks. The next time the panel would re-render that file it re-hashes
the body, finds it no longer matches the header, and **stops**. The site is
marked as drifted, and the panel shows you a diff between what is on disk and
what it would have written. You then choose:

- **Keep my edit** — the panel leaves it alone. It will keep telling you the
  file has drifted, because it can no longer manage that site's configuration.
- **Discard my edit** — the panel re-renders and overwrites. This is the only
  path that overwrites, and it is never taken without being asked.

Deleting a site removes its vhost whether or not it has drifted: you asked for
the site to go away.

## The escape hatches

Editing a generated file is usually the wrong tool, because these exist and
survive a re-render:

| What you want | Where it lives |
|---|---|
| Extra nginx directives for one site | **Custom snippet** on the site, rendered inside the `server` block |
| Different `memory_limit`, `upload_max_filesize`, … | **PHP overrides** on the site, appended to its pool |
| Larger uploads | `client_max_body_size` on the site |
| A maintenance page | The maintenance toggle |

A custom snippet is validated by `nginx -t` before it is activated. If it is
wrong, the change is rejected with nginx's own error message — file, line number
and all — and the previous configuration is still what is running.

## What happens on every change

1. The new file is rendered from a template. A missing value is a **render
   failure**, not an empty string, so a renamed field can never produce
   `server_name ;` — a vhost that would swallow every request on the server.
2. The current file is snapshotted.
3. The new file is written atomically: a temporary file in the same directory,
   fsynced, then renamed. A power cut leaves the old file, never half the new
   one.
4. The service's own checker runs — `nginx -t`, `php-fpm8.3 -t`. **Writing the
   file changes nothing about the running server; only the reload does**, which
   is why validation happens here rather than earlier.
5. On failure, the snapshot is restored byte for byte and you get the checker's
   output. Nothing was reloaded.
6. On success, the service is reloaded — not restarted, so no connection is
   dropped.
7. The activation is stored as a revision, and any revision can be put back in
   one click.

Two sites being created at once cannot interleave: rendering is serialised per
service, so a validation never runs against a half-written tree.

## Files Ferrum does not own

`nginx.conf`, `sites-enabled`, the distribution's stock pool files. The panel's
entire footprint on files it did not create is a single line in
`/etc/nginx/conf.d/ferrum.conf`:

```nginx
include /etc/nginx/ferrum.d/*.conf;
```

That is why `apt upgrade nginx` and a panel upgrade do not interact.

## If the panel is down

Your sites keep serving. Nginx, PHP-FPM and the databases are ordinary systemd
units reading ordinary files, and neither Ferrum process is in the request path.
